Q3'26.headline: Revenue of US$46.7B (+16.2% QoQ, +41% YoY in US$) beat the top of the US$44.6-45.8B guide; in NT dollars it rose 17.6% QoQ and 50.9% YoY to NT$1,494.2B. Gross margin fell 1.3pp QoQ to 66.4%, inside the 65-67% guide, as the N2 ramp diluted margins. EPS was NT$29.43 (+68.7% YoY). TSMC guided Q4'26 revenue to US$52.3-54.3B (+58% YoY at the midpoint), raised FY2026 US$ growth to around 44% and reiterated 2026 capex of US$60-64B.

points.text: CFO Wendell Huang said the 130bp sequential gross-margin drop to 66.4% was mainly due to dilution from the initial N2 ramp. He now expects overseas-fab dilution to be closer to 2% for full-year 2026, widening to 3-4% over the next few years as more US fabs ramp.

CEO C.C. Wei said agentic AI and open-source models are fueling AI demand, which adds demand for agentic AI CPUs and networking chips on top of accelerators. Asked about the mid-to-high-50s AI accelerator CAGR (2024-2029), he said it 'probably will be higher' and that TSMC sees no sign of slowdown.

Huang reiterated 2026 capex of US$60-64B and said 2026-2028 capex will be 'even more significantly higher' than the prior three years. Wei said TSMC has nearly 20 fabs in progress: 13 leading-edge and advanced packaging fabs in Taiwan and 5-6 overseas.

Wei expects N2-family annual capacity to more than double in 2027. A14 risk production is on track for 2027 and volume production for 2028, with more customer activity than N2 had at this stage. TSMC added a fourth N3 fab (another Tainan fab, volume production 1H28) and pulled Arizona fab 2 (N3) volume production into 3Q27.

Wei said TSMC is looking beyond Arizona, including Texas, for more US capacity, and that any new fab 'got to be run by TSMC'. He also said TSMC sends its own teams to check US data-center build-out and power supply, and the feedback is 'so far so good'.

Wei said rising component prices and macro uncertainty are hurting consumer and price-sensitive end markets, so TSMC is 'being prudent' in planning for 2027. Leading-edge demand, he said, remains 'extremely robust'.

guidance: Q4'26 revenue US$52.3-54.3B (+14% QoQ, +58% YoY at midpoint)
Q4'26 gross margin 65-67%; operating margin 56.5-58.5%; assumes US$1 = NT$31.8
FY2026 revenue growth around 44% YoY in US$ (raised from slightly above 40%)
FY2026 capex US$60-64B reiterated; 2026-2028 capex significantly higher than the prior three years
FY2026 overseas-fab gross-margin dilution closer to 2%, widening to 3-4% in the next few years
qa: Laura (analyst; firm not identified in the transcript) asked whether the mid-to-high-50s AI accelerator CAGR still holds given power and funding concerns; C.C. Wei said demand is 'extremely robust' with no sign of slowdown and the CAGR 'probably will be higher'. On margins, he said there is 'no ceiling' but no dramatic increase overnight.

Gokul Hariharan (JPMorgan) asked about 2027 supply tightness and US expansion (Texas, a customer's fab project); Wei said US sites beyond Arizona are under study and any fab must be run by TSMC. Huang said it is too early to give capacity growth rates.

Krish Sankar (TD Cowen) asked about customers reselling wafer allocations and the 2030 High-NA EUV timing; Wei said TSMC does not allow customers to sublet or auction capacity. TSMC will adopt High-NA around 2030, once the tool is mature and cost-effective.

Charlie Chan (Morgan Stanley) asked about an IDM customer insourcing and about packaging competition; Wei said A14 customer engagement exceeds N2's so far and TSMC is the only company producing 5x-reticle packages today.

Sunny Lin (UBS) asked about 2027 capex and tool inflation; Huang said tool, material and labor inflation is real but revenue growth should still outpace capex growth. He added that the 3-4% overseas dilution applies to the later part of the five-year period.
Arthur Lai (Macquarie) asked whether CPUs are in the AI accelerator definition; Wei said no, because TSMC cannot tell which CPUs go into AI servers.

Q2'26.headline: Revenue of US$40.2B came in at the top of the US$39.0-40.2B guide (NT$1,270.4B, +36.0% YoY). Gross margin of 67.7% beat the 65.5-67.5% range on cost improvements and higher utilization, and EPS rose 77.4% YoY to NT$27.25. TSMC raised 2026 capex to US$60-64B, lifted FY2026 US$ growth to slightly above 40% and announced another US$100B for Arizona. It guided Q3'26 to US$44.6-45.8B with a margin dip from the N2 ramp.

points.text: CFO Wendell Huang raised the 2026 capital budget to US$60-64B, from 'towards the high end' of US$52-56B, citing strong structural demand that includes agentic AI. In Q&A, C.C. Wei gave two reasons: rising customer demand and tool price inflation.

Wei announced an additional US$100B investment in Arizona for several more fabs for 2nm and below plus advanced packaging, taking the US total to US$265B. He said this means 'probably additional 4 or more fabs'.

Huang guided Q3'26 gross margin down 1.7pp to 66% at the midpoint, mainly because the steep N2 ramp should dilute gross margin by about 3-4pp in 2H26. Overseas dilution is still forecast at 2-3% in the early stages, widening to 3-4% later.

Wei said agentic AI is 'leading to a resurgence in the role of CPUs in AI data centers', and that x86, Arm and RISC-V CPU designers are almost all TSMC customers. Asked about the AI CAGR, he said demand is 'stronger than what we said before' but gave no new number.

Wei introduced A13, an optical shrink of A14 with backward-compatible design rules, and A12, which adds Super Power Rail to the A14 platform; both target volume production in 2029. A14 itself is scheduled for volume production in 2028, and customer tape-out activity is ahead of schedule.

Wei said mature-node demand outside power management ICs and CMOS image sensors 'is not that strong'. The AI-linked shortage is in PMICs and sensors, and TSMC keeps adding specialty capacity at JASM (Japan) and ESMC (Germany).

qa: Sunny Lin (UBS) asked for a 2026-2028 capex guide and the Arizona timeline; Huang gave no number but said TSMC is 'stepping up' capex. Wei said the extra US$100B means probably 4 or more additional fabs, with timing tied to the market.
Charlie Chan (Morgan Stanley) asked about Samsung, Intel and the AI CAGR; Wei said there are no shortcuts in foundry and AI demand is getting 'stronger and stronger', but gave no new number.

Arthur Lai (Macquarie) and Haas Liu (Bank of America) asked about Intel's EMIB-T packaging; Wei said TSMC's packaging capacity is so tight that he welcomes alternatives, because they help TSMC's front-end wafer business.
Gokul Hariharan asked how TSMC vets customer forecasts; Wei said 'All the truth together is not a truth'. He believes demand stays very strong through 2029-2030, possibly with a dip in between.
Jim Fontanelli (Arete) asked about customer concentration and vendor financing; Wei said concentration is not a concern and TSMC does not make financial arrangements with customers.
Felix Pan (KGI) asked what drove the capex raise from US$52-56B to US$60-64B; Wei cited rising customer demand first and tool price inflation second.

points.text: C.C. Wei raised FY2026 revenue growth to above 30% in US$ (from close to 30%), citing 'extremely robust' AI demand as agentic AI drives another step-up in token consumption. He flagged rising component prices and the Middle East situation as risks for consumer segments.

Wei announced a global plan for three new N3 fabs: a new fab in Tainan (volume production 1H27), Arizona fab 2 (2H27) and Japan fab 2 (2028), plus continued conversion of N5 tools to N3. Wendell Huang said 2026 capex will be towards the high end of US$52-56B.

Huang guided Q2'26 gross margin to 66.5% at the midpoint and repeated that N2 will dilute full-year margin by 2-3%, starting in 2H26. N3 should cross the corporate average margin in 2H26. Middle East-driven chemical and gas price increases may affect profitability, but it is too early to quantify the impact.
Wei said TSMC plans to wind down Fab 2 (6-inch) and Fab 5 (8-inch), exit gallium nitride, and reuse the space to support leading-edge applications. Existing customers will still be fully supported.

Asked about the Intel/Tesla 'terafab' plan, Wei said both are TSMC customers and 'we view Intel as a formidable competitor and do not underestimate them', but 'there are no shortcuts' in the foundry business.

points.text: C.C. Wei forecast 2026 revenue growth of close to 30% in US$, versus 14% growth for the 'Foundry 2.0' industry. He also raised the long-term outlook: AI accelerator revenue to approach a mid-to-high-50s CAGR and total revenue to approach a 25% CAGR in US$ over 2024-2029.

Wendell Huang set 2026 capex at US$52-56B (vs US$40.9B in 2025), 70-80% for advanced process. Depreciation should rise by a high-teens percentage in 2026. He said capex over the past three years totaled US$101B and is 'expected to be significantly higher in the next three years'.

Huang raised the long-term gross-margin target to '56% and higher through the cycle' (from 53% and higher) and set an ROE target of high-20s through the cycle. He said N2 will dilute 2026 gross margin by 2-3%, starting in 2H26.
Huang said 'Our pricing will remain strategic, not opportunistic, to earn our value', citing much higher capex per k-wafers for N2 than for N3, and even higher for A14.

Wei said Arizona fab 2 (N3) volume production was pulled into 2H27, construction of fab 3 has started, and TSMC bought a second large land parcel. He said Arizona yield and defect density are almost equal to Taiwan's.
Huang said advanced packaging was slightly over 10% of 2025 revenue (about 8% in 2024) and should reach low-teens percent in 2026, growing faster than the corporate average.

points.text: Wendell Huang said every 1% NT dollar appreciation cuts reported NT revenue by about 1% and gross margin by about 40bp. The Q2 rate (NT$31.05 vs NT$32.88 in Q1) cost about 220bp of margin, and Arizona dilution added slightly over 100bp. He still saw a long-term gross margin of 53% and higher as 'well achievable'.

C.C. Wei raised FY2025 revenue growth to around 30% in US$ (from close to mid-20s percent), citing strong AI demand including sovereign AI. He remained mindful of tariff risks to consumer and price-sensitive segments.

Wei detailed the US$165B US plan: six wafer fabs, two advanced packaging fabs and an R&D center in Arizona, with about 30% of 2nm-and-more-advanced capacity eventually in Arizona. Arizona fab 2 (N3) construction is complete and its schedule is being pulled in by several quarters.
Wei said N3 and N5 capacity will stay 'very tight' for a couple of years as AI products migrate from 4nm to 3nm. Huang said N2's structural profitability is better than N3's.
Huang kept 2025 capex at US$38-42B despite the higher revenue outlook, citing macro uncertainty. He said TSMC will not hesitate to invest as long as business opportunities exist.

thesis.summary: TSMC is the world's dominant contract chipmaker: it manufactures logic wafers, and increasingly packages them, for GPU, custom-ASIC, CPU and smartphone chip designers (more than 500 customers), earning almost all revenue in US dollars while reporting in NT dollars. Technology leadership at each new node (N3 now, N2 ramping since 4Q25, A14 in 2028) lets it charge premium wafer prices and run very high utilization, which drove gross margin from 58.6% in Q2'25 to 66-68% in 2026. AI accelerators were a high-teens share of 2025 revenue, and management sees them growing at a mid-to-high-50s CAGR (2024-2029) and total revenue at approaching 25% a year, so HPC has risen to 68% of revenue. The market debates whether the step-up in capex (US$60-64B in 2026, 'significantly higher' in 2026-2028) is matched by durable AI demand, how far overseas fabs and new-node ramps dilute margins, NT dollar swings, and Taiwan-concentrated geopolitical risk.

pillars.title: Sole-source leading edge for AI
pillars.text: Nearly every AI accelerator, custom ASIC and now agentic-AI CPU is built on TSMC's N5/N3/N2 and packaged with its CoWoS. Management describes demand as exceeding supply through at least 2027, and the shortage is front-end and back-end at once.

evidence.text: HPC rose to 68% of revenue in Q3'26 (+22% QoQ), from 60% in Q2'25
AI accelerator revenue CAGR raised to mid-to-high 50s for 2024-2029 (from mid-40s); Wei said in Oct 2026 it 'probably will be higher'
FY2026 US$ revenue growth guide raised four times: close to 30% -> above 30% -> slightly above 40% -> around 44%

pillars.title: Structurally higher profitability
pillars.text: Gross margin moved from 58.6% (Q2'25) to 67.7% (Q2'26) through high utilization, cost improvements, N3 maturing and 'strategic, not opportunistic' pricing. In January 2026 the long-term floor was raised to 56%+ through the cycle.

evidence.text: Long-term gross margin target raised to 56% and higher from 53% and higher; ROE high-20s through the cycle
Q1'26 gross margin of 66.2% beat the high end of guidance by 120bp; Q4'25 by 130bp; Q3'25 by 200bp
Operating margin 60.3% in Q2'26 vs 49.6% in Q2'25

pillars.title: Node cadence keeps the moat widening
pillars.text: N2 entered volume production in 4Q25 and is ramping faster than N3, with capacity set to more than double in 2027. A14 (2028), A13/A12 (2029) and High-NA around 2030 extend the roadmap, and A14 is drawing more customer engagement than N2 at the same stage.

evidence.text: N2 went from 3% of wafer revenue in Q2'26 to 8% in Q3'26
N2-family annual capacity expected to more than double in 2027; A14 risk production 2027, volume 2028

pillars.title: Capex funded from cash flow, with dividends rising
pillars.text: Even with capex stepping up to US$60-64B, operating cash flow covers capex with room for a growing dividend. Management's rule is that revenue growth should outpace capex growth.

evidence.text: Q3'26 operating cash flow ~NT$920B vs capex NT$443B
Dividend per share NT$14 (2024) -> NT$18 (2025) -> NT$24 (2026), with a further increase expected in 2027
FY2025 FCF NT$1T (+15.2%) on capex of US$40.9B

segments.name: HPC (AI accelerators, CPUs, networking)
segments.text: The largest and fastest-growing platform, covering GPUs, custom AI ASICs, server and now agentic-AI CPUs, and networking chips. HPC grew 48% in 2025 to 58% of revenue and reached 68% in Q3'26. Management keeps the AI accelerator definition narrow (GPU, ASIC, HBM controller) and excludes CPUs.

themes.text: Each quarter management said AI demand was stronger than three months before and raised the CAGR.
themes.quote: All I can say right now is the demand is very extremely robust.

themes.theme: AI accelerators already a large slice
themes.text: First disclosure of the AI share of revenue came with the Q4'25 results.
themes.quote: Revenue from AI accelerators accounted for high-teens percent of our total revenue in 2025.

themes.text: Agentic workloads add CPU and networking demand on top of accelerators; almost all CPU designers are TSMC customers.
themes.quote: The emergence of agentic AI is leading to a resurgence in the role of CPUs in AI data centers, which drive more silicon demand in addition to AI accelerators.

themes.text: TSMC now vets forecasts directly with cloud providers and even sends teams to check data-center and power build-outs.
themes.quote: we directly receive very strong signals from our customers' customers, requesting the capacity to support their business.

segments.name: Smartphone
segments.text: Historically TSMC's largest platform and still the lead customer base for each new node (N2 ramps on both smartphone and HPC). Smartphone grew 11% in 2025 to 29% of revenue, but its share fell to 21% in Q3'26 as HPC surged. Rising memory and component prices are the main 2026-2027 risk.

themes.text: Management has flagged memory and component price increases for three straight quarters.
themes.quote: Memory price hike definitely has some impact to, uh, price-sensitive end market, especially in PC and smartphone market.

themes.text: TSMC's customers skew to premium phones and PCs, which are less sensitive to component costs.
themes.quote: most of my customers now focus on high-end smartphone or PCs, so those kind of demand has less sensitive to the component price.

segments.name: IoT, automotive and DCE
segments.text: Smaller platforms (about 5%, 4-5% and 1% of revenue) built mostly on mature and specialty nodes. Automotive grew 34% and IoT 15% in 2025. Edge-AI devices add silicon content through larger die sizes rather than unit growth.

themes.theme: Edge AI raises die size, not units
themes.text: On-device AI adoption shows up as larger dies.
themes.quote: the increase on the edge device, the number of the units is actually mild, but the die size increased.

segments.name: Leading-edge nodes (N2, N3, A14)
segments.text: 7nm and below rose from 74% of wafer revenue in 2025 to 79% in Q3'26. N3 is so tight that TSMC broke its rule of not adding capacity to a mature node, adding four N3 fabs (Tainan x2, Arizona, Japan). N2 is ramping steeply, diluting gross margin by 3-4pp in 2H26, and A14 is set to be an even bigger node.

themes.text: AI demand migrating from 4nm to 3nm led TSMC to build new N3 fabs.
themes.quote: Historically, we do not add additional capacity to one node once it reaches its target capacity.

themes.theme: N2 bigger and faster than N3
themes.text: N2 ramps on both smartphone and HPC from the start.
themes.quote: We expect our N2 family technologies annual capacity to more than double in 2027, supported by strong demand from both smartphone and HPC AI applications.

themes.theme: A14 already drawing more interest than N2
themes.text: A14 (volume 2028) plus the A13/A12 derivatives (2029) extend the roadmap.
themes.quote: Actually, in our A14, we have seen more and more customers actually higher than the 2 nanometer activities so far.

segments.name: Advanced packaging (CoWoS, SoIC)
segments.text: Advanced packaging rose from about 8% of revenue in 2024 to slightly over 10% in 2025 and is guided to low-teens percent in 2026, growing faster than the company. Capacity is short, so TSMC works with OSATs (including an Arizona OSAT and GlobalFoundries for interposers) and tolerates rivals' packaging such as Intel's EMIB-T.

themes.text: Back-end capacity is as tight as front-end, so TSMC relies on partners.
themes.quote: let me say that our advanced packaging capacity is very tight also.

themes.theme: Packaging growing faster than the company
themes.text: Wendell Huang gave the first revenue share and outlook.
themes.quote: We expect it to grow faster than the corporate average, and account for low-teens % in 2026.

segments.name: Mature and specialty nodes
segments.text: 16nm and older nodes are a shrinking share of revenue. TSMC is pruning commodity capacity (winding down 6-inch Fab 2 and 8-inch Fab 5, exiting GaN) while adding specialty capacity at JASM (image sensors) and ESMC (automotive/industrial). The AI-linked tightness is in power management ICs and sensors.

themes.text: The strategy is to avoid China-driven mature-node overcapacity by focusing on differentiated processes.
themes.quote: Our focus is to build high-yield capacity for specialized technologies rather than just normal capacity.

themes.theme: Only AI-linked mature demand is tight
themes.text: PMICs and sensors for AI data centers are short; other areas are weak.
themes.quote: In today's market, outside of specific areas such as power management IC and CMOS image sensor, The mature node demand in other commodity areas is not that strong.

segments.name: Overseas fabs (Arizona, Japan, Germany)
segments.text: Total US commitment reached US$265B after an extra US$100B in July 2026, enough for 4 or more more Arizona fabs, and TSMC is studying sites beyond Arizona. Overseas fabs dilute gross margin, by about 2% in 2026 and widening to 3-4% in later years, but US customers want the capacity.

themes.text: Fab 2 (N3) volume production was pulled into 3Q27, with N2/A16 fabs to follow.
themes.quote: we would like to announce an additional $100 billion investment in Arizona.

themes.text: The margin cost of overseas fabs grows as more US fabs ramp.
themes.quote: we expect the dilution from our overseas fabs to widen to 3-4% in the next few years.

risks.text: Currency: nearly all revenue is in US$ while about 75% of COGS is in NT$; each 1% NT$ appreciation cuts NT revenue about 1% and gross margin about 40bp (Q2'25 lost about 220bp of margin to FX).

Capex overbuild if AI demand stalls: 2026 capex is US$60-64B and 2026-2028 will be 'significantly higher' than the US$101B spent in 2023-2025. Wei said a careless plan 'will be a big disaster to TSMC'.
Margin dilution from the N2 ramp (3-4pp in 2H26) and overseas fabs (widening to 3-4% in later years), plus tool, material and labor inflation.

Supply chain and energy: the Middle East situation raised chemical and gas prices, and Taiwan's LNG supply was secured only through May 2026 at the time of the Q1'26 call. Wei said he worries about electricity in Taiwan first.
Competition: Intel (with US government and customer backing, plus the Intel/Tesla 'terafab' plan), Samsung and alternative packaging (EMIB-T) could take share while TSMC's capacity is constrained.
Consumer weakness: rising memory and component prices are 'challenging' smartphone, PC and other price-sensitive segments heading into 2027.

debates.q: Is the AI capex cycle durable enough to justify TSMC's capex step-up?
debates.bull: TSMC checks demand with its customers' customers and data-center build-outs, raised the AI CAGR to mid-to-high 50s, says it will 'probably be higher', and sees supply short until new fabs arrive in 2028-2029.
debates.bear: Customer forecasts are aggressive ('All the truth together is not a truth'), Wei admits a possible dip before 2029-2030, and capex is locked in years ahead.

debates.q: Can gross margin stay well above the 56% long-term floor?
debates.bull: Margins of 66-68% in 2026 came despite N2 and overseas dilution; N3 is turning accretive, pricing is 'strategic', and Wei says 'there's no ceiling for TSMC's profitability'.
debates.bear: N2 and A14 cost far more per k-wafers, overseas dilution widens to 3-4%, tools are inflating, and the NT dollar can swing margins by several points.

debates.q: Does Intel or Samsung foundry become a real second source?
debates.bull: Wei says 'there are no shortcuts': technology, manufacturing excellence and trust take years, and A14 engagement exceeds N2's.
debates.bear: Intel has government and customer backing, a big customer is planning its own fab capacity, and TSMC's tight capacity pushes customers to qualify alternatives.

debates.q: Is the US expansion value-accretive or a political cost?
debates.bull: US customers request the capacity and value geographic flexibility; Arizona yields match Taiwan's and pricing can differ by location.
debates.bear: US$265B committed with 2-4% gross-margin dilution, with further sites (Texas) under study.
